title: Discovering date formats in Spreadsheets using Python
text:
When the date variable has multiple formats for dates. Such as ['Mar-2023','01-01-2021', '01/05/2020','01-Apr-2021', ...] converting to date using the standard command pd.to_datetime() is complicated. It will throw an error because of the different formats and if you chose to ignore and force fix then you will lose information.
Luckily this is a problem that is fading away fast with better data collection systems. But I have come across spreadsheets with date in all different formats. This becomes a problem when the dateset is large. I have seen this in the past when I was working with a large dataset of 100,000 rows and the date variable had multiple formats.
I’m sure there are other ways to solve but I would use the following simple approach. I used regex to replace the digits with letters such as “a” or “b” or anything else, then, I do a value_counts() on this variable. This way I can learn the different date formats in the dataset and then I can fix them accordingly.
Suppose you have the following date variable with multiple formats:

import pandas as pd

# let's say you have a date variable with multiple formats
date_list = ['Mar-2023',
 '01-01-2021',
 '01/05/2020',
 '01-Apr-2021',
 '10-Feb-2020',
 '01-03-2021',
 'Apr-2023',
 '20/07/2019',
 'Dec-2023',]

# Create a DataFrame
dt = pd.DataFrame({'Date': date_list})

print(dt)

          Date
0     Mar-2023
1   01-01-2021
2   01/05/2020
3  01-Apr-2021
4  10-Feb-2020
5   01-03-2021
6     Apr-2023
7   20/07/2019
8     Dec-2023


In order to learn the different formats so you can fix them, I use regex like this - first, I replace the digits with letters such as “a” or “b” or anything else, then, I do a value_counts() on this variable. For example:

# You can use regex to learn the different formats.
dt.Date.str.replace(r'\d',"z", regex=True).value_counts()

Date
zz-zz-zzzz     2
zz/zz/zzzz     2
Mar-zzzz       1
zz-Apr-zzzz    1
zz-Feb-zzzz    1
Apr-zzzz       1
Dec-zzzz       1
Name: count, dtype: int64


This way I can see the different date formats in the dataset and then I can fix them accordingly. Hope this helps you when you are working with date variables with multiple formats.

title: On Debit and Credit transactions in the banking system - part 1
text:
RBI’s Bankwise ATM/POS/Card Statistics data
The Bankwise ATM/POS/Card Statistics is a collection of spreadsheets with monthly indicators of some banking statistics, such as the number of ATMs, active credit and debit cards, monthly volume and value of payments on debit and credit transactions, across all banks operating in the country. The data goes back to the 2000s and are available here on the RBI website.


Downloading the data
Below is the code to scrape the links to the spreadsheets from the RBI website and download them. The code uses requests and BeautifulSoup to extract the links to the spreadsheets, filters for only those that end with “XLSX”, and then downloads each file using urllib.request.urlretrieve.

from bs4 import BeautifulSoup
import requests

url = "https://rbi.org.in/scripts/atmview.aspx"
response = requests.get(url)
soup = BeautifulSoup(response.content, 'html.parser')

# Extract links from td elements
links = []
for td in soup.find_all('td'):
    link = td.find('a')
    if link and link.get('href'):
        links.append({
            'text': link.get_text(strip=True),
            'href': link['href']
        })

With the links extracted, we can create a DataFrame and filter for only those that end with “XLSX”, which are the spreadsheets we want to download.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

dt=pd.DataFrame(links)
dt['text']=dt['text'].replace(r'^\s*$', np.nan, regex=True).ffill()
dt= dt[dt.href.str.endswith("XLSX")]

To download the files using the links extracted above, we write fetch_data function that takes a URL and an optional file name, and uses urllib.request.urlretrieve to download the file. The loop iterates over the filtered links and downloads each spreadsheet.

import urllib.request    
def fetch_data(url, file_name=None):
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, file_name )

for links in dt.href:
    print(links)
    fil = links.split("/")[-1]
    fetch_data(links, fil)



Pain points in using the data
The 2025 spreadsheets are largely standardized, however, the data is organized in a way that is not immediately machine-readable. Multiple levels of hierarchical column headings and metadata embedded in the file names and sheet names make it difficult to parse the data quickly for further analysis. The overhead of processing could be discouraging. It’d be ideal if RBI restructures or at least shares a format that is machine-readable so more effort is directed towards using the data in interesting ways.
Multi-level column names
While informative the multi-level columns are a pain to parse and work with. The multi-level columns names had to be compressed into concise variable names. I did this manually. I created a CSV file var_name.csv, which is essentially a lookup/metadata table that maps the verbose hierarchical column headings used in the RBI spreadsheets to concise variable names used in the analysis.

import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px
# read the column names file
col_names = pd.read_csv("var_name.csv")
col_dict = col_names["col_name"].to_list()
col_dict = ['bank_name'] + col_dict 
print(col_names[['B', 'C', 'E','col_name']].head())

                                        B                C         E  \
0  Number - Outstanding (as on month end)      ATMs & CRMs   On-site   
1  Number - Outstanding (as on month end)      ATMs & CRMs  Off-site   
2  Number - Outstanding (as on month end)              PoS       NaN   
3  Number - Outstanding (as on month end)       Micro ATMs       NaN   
4  Number - Outstanding (as on month end)  Bharat QR Codes       NaN   

           col_name  
0   on_site_atms_no  
1  off_site_atms_no  
2            pos_no  
3     micro_atms_no  
4   bharat_codes_no  


Bank type: Private, public, foreign banks
The banks are grouped by their type: private, public or foreign sector banks. The type information is a row separator dividing the banks. To incorporate this information in the tabular dataset, I created another file where the bank names were mapped to their respective type. This file is called bank_sector_map.csv. This file has two columns: bank_name and type (with values ‘private’, ‘public’, ‘foreign’). The advantage of this approach is that it creates a separate table in a database sense and makes it easy to add new bank level information or for adding new banks into the fold.

# Import and merge bank_sector_map.csv
bank_sector_map = pd.read_csv("bank_sector_map.csv")
bank_sector_map.rename(columns={'type':'bank_type'}, inplace=True)
print(bank_sector_map.head())

  bank_type              bank_name
0    public         BANK OF BARODA
1    public          BANK OF INDIA
2    public    BANK OF MAHARASHTRA
3    public            CANARA BANK
4    public  CENTRAL BANK OF INDIA


There are 64 banks in the dataset, and here is the distribution of the types of banks in the data:

print(bank_sector_map.bank_type.value_counts())

bank_type
private          21
foreign          14
public           12
small_finance    11
payment           6
Name: count, dtype: int64


bank_type is an important variable that can be used to compare the performance of private vs public sector banks in terms of their ATM/POS/Card statistics. This variable can be used to analyze if there are any differences in the trends of transactions between private and public sector banks.
Month-Year of the data
This information was embedded in the sheet name or file name in a non-standardized way (sometimes “May2025” and other times as “202512” in the file name that looks like ATM122025010824B80F314664BFB1DA8F17935161.XLSX). I had to extract this information from the sheet name (below) and create a new variable time_period to capture the month-year of the data for each row. This is crucial for any time series analysis or trend analysis over time.


Combining the monthly data
Below is the code for combining the monthly data from the multiple spreadsheets into a single DataFrame for analysis. The function func_combine reads each spreadsheet (ignore the headers from the top and some footnote), processes it to extract the relevant data, rename the columns and then loop through all the files into a single DataFrame dat0.

# write a function to read multiple files and combine the data

def func_combine(path2file):
    dat1 = pd.read_excel(path2file,
    index_col=0,
    usecols="B:AC",
    skiprows=9,
    skipfooter=28
    )
    dat1 = dat1.dropna(axis=1, how="all")
    # add column to grab meta data in filename
    sheetname = pd.ExcelFile(path2file).sheet_names[0]
    dat1['file_name'] =  sheetname
    # rename column names
    old_new = dict(zip(dat1.columns.to_list(), col_dict))
    dat1.rename(columns=old_new, inplace=True)
    dat1.reset_index(drop=True, inplace=True)
    return dat1

Applying the function to all files in the directory that match the pattern “ATM…XLSX”

from pathlib import Path
import glob
fdata = Path(".")
flist=list(fdata.glob("*ATM*"))
dat0 = pd.DataFrame()
for file1 in flist:
    dat1 = func_combine(file1)
    dat0 = pd.concat([dat0,dat1])



Cleaning the data
Grab the time period from the sheet names
After removing some rows that held totals across banks on different variables, I extracted and added month-year to the data. The month and year of the data were embedded in the sheet names, which were in this format “For Website April 2025” or similar. These were extracted and then converted to datetime format like ‘April 2025’ or similar.

dat0.dropna(subset=['bank_name'], inplace=True)
dat0['time_period']=dat0.file_name.str.replace("For Website ", "")

try:
    dat0['time_period'] = pd.to_datetime(dat0['time_period'], format='%B %Y')
except Exception:
    # fallback to pandas' parser
    dat0['time_period'] = pd.to_datetime(dat0['time_period'], errors='coerce')
    if dat0['time_period'].isna().any():
        print("Warning: some time_period values could not be parsed and are NaT")

Add type of bank: private, public or foreign
Mapping the bank names to their respective sectors (private, public, foreign) using the bank_sector_map.csv file that we created earlier. This will allow us to analyze the data by bank type.

# Import and merge bank_sector_map.csv
bank_sector_map = pd.read_csv("bank_sector_map.csv")
dat0 = dat0.merge(bank_sector_map, on='bank_name', how='left')

Here is a quick look at the data after cleaning and merging. Note that there were some duplicate column names in the original data, which I checked for and removed if any.
The final DataFrame dat0 should have unique column names and be ready for analysis.

dat0.head()
dat0 = dat0.sort_values(by='time_period', ascending=True)
dat0.to_csv("combined_atm_data.csv", index=False)
print("Data combined, cleaned and saved. Sample rows:\n", dat0.head())

title: India 2026: Bonds over Equities?
text:
Geopolitical events with no clear end in sight, tectonic shifts in technology, and the vie for its hegemony by the power-hungry is rewriting investment decisions around the world. This churn will increase volatility further in the equity markets. Looking for capital preservation with predictable returns in 2026 is completely reasonable and recommended.

Waning interest of FIIs
Since 2024, FIIs have been selling indian equities. In 2025 they net sold Rs 1.2 lac crore, and in the first three months of 2026, they offloaded Rs 1 lac crore (exceeding 2025’s trends). FIIs ignored the GST reduction, the strong corporate earnings, the improving economic indicators, as well the various growth-inducive measures announced in the Union Budget FY2027 and the recent India-EU free trade agreement (FTA). They have sold on the backdrop of a falling rupee indicating no revival in the rupee in the short run or medium term - implying the dollar will remain strong for the foreseeable future making indian equities less attractive for foreign investors.


Liquidity tightening
To stall the falling rupee, RBI intervened on several ocassions - sold dollars and bought rupees. These interventions come at a cost. It sucks liquidity out of the market. While RBI infused liquidity back into the system via OMO of about Rs 4.2 trillion, and maintained soft stance on interest rates, the liquidity conditions is getting tight.
Yields have experienced an upward trend since November 2025, with the benchmark 10-year yield rising from around 6.54% in November 2025 to over 6.8% by late March 2026, hitting 16-month highs. High Credit-deposit ratios in the banking sector and cash demand will continue to put pressure on liquidity in the system, which will continue to push bond yields higher. RBI recently cancelled two T-Bill issuance on account of elevated bids. Front-loading government borrowing in the first quarter of the coming FY will further push yields higher.


West Asia conflict, energy prices
The Israel-US-Iran conflict has destabilized the middle east, shocked the energy supply chain and pushed energy prices up. It will remain so for the near to medium term, and we are yet to see or assess the impact of the instability in the middle east, the strained relationships due to Iran’s retaliation. The energy dynamics in this region will heighten uncertainty around india’s energy supplies and prices. Higher energy prices will put pressure on inflation whether or not it is passed through fully. The effects will surface in the next few months.


Inflation expectations, interest rate pressure
High inflation due to energy prices will likely push RBI towards a more hawkish stance. To rein inflation expectations, we might see rate hikes in the coming months. Higher interest rates will dampen sentiments, demand, and earnings.
Even if the cascade of events become less negative, it is unlikely the Indian equity markets will show a promising year. Weakening rupee, geopolitical frictions, FIIs on the sidelines, and exaggerated valuation of indian stocks will generate likely keep equity markets muted.


Attractiveness of Bonds, potential tax reliefs
Higher bond yields will be an attractive option for capital preservation in the medium term (2-3 years.) At the moment, fixed income returns have complicated tax compliance needs. They are treated differently than equity market gains. However, there has been a lot of noise in the financial community to level the playing field between equity and fixed income gains. If this happens, it will make bonds even more attractive.
Investing in government bonds and highly rated corporate bonds for capital preservation and predictable returns in 2026 is a wise choice.

title: Installing Spark/PySpark/Spark-NLP
text:
For a project dealing with medical notes, I wanted to experiment with a spark-nlp package put out by the John Snow Labs. The main objective of the task was to detect symptoms in clinical notes. Below are the steps used to set up the foundation for using the spark-nlp package.



Downloaded Spark (3.1.3 Prebuilt for Hadoop3.2)

Unzipped to ~/Documents/

Added the following lines to .zshrc file

export SPARK_HOME="/Users/sandeep/Documents/spark-3.1.3-bin-hadoop3.2"
export PYSPARK_PYTHON=python3
export PYSPARK_DRIVER_PYTHON="jupyter"
export PYSPARK_DRIVER_PYTHON_OPTS="notebook"

Create a new conda environment with python=3.8 (numpy and pandas)

conda create --name myenv python=3.8 pandas numpy

Activate the new environment to install the following

conda activate myenv

Install pyspark

conda install -c conda-forge pyspark

Installed spark-nlp

conda install -c johnsnowlabs spark-nlp

Activate the python environment created above, i.e. myenv and then type pyspark in the console. It should open with Jupyter
If all good, create a new notebook and run some sparky commands from the tutorial etc.

title: Installing Spark/PySpark/Spark-NLP
section: pyspark and spark-nlp from John Snow Labs
text:
pyspark and spark-nlp from John Snow Labs
The main challenge for pyspark and spark-nlp was for pyspark to pick up .jar files from spark-nlp. These should be in the PATH. But there was a work around. When working with a specific package, you can fire up pyspark from terminal as below
pyspark --packages com.johnsnowlabs.nlp:spark-nlp_2.12:3.1.3
In my example I was working wih com.johnsnowlabs.nlp:spark-nlp_2.12:3.1.3 package. You can replace with the one you are interested in.
